claims.head: Who drives the play: the Bruins
claims.body: The Bruins have been around the middle of the league at controlling the chances at 5-on-5, and the Maple Leafs one of the worst. Expect the Bruins to spend more of the night in the Maple Leafs’ end. That’s about the puck, not the scoreboard: goalies and finishing decide plenty of games the chances don’t.

notes.text: Kirill Marchenko is day to day (lower body injury) and has missed the last 10 games. He is one of their most valuable skaters. Easton Cowan has taken his spot beside Jack Roslovic and Auston Matthews. That line has had 45% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 81:47 together, down from 72% with Marchenko.

Nick Blankenburg is on injured reserve (upper-body injury) and has missed the last 12 games. He is one of their more valuable skaters. Troy Stecher has taken his spot beside Oliver Ekman-Larsson. That pair has had 52% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 71:15 together, about what it had with Blankenburg (48%).
Ryan Tverberg was added to the roster on Nov 12 and has played beside John Tavares and William Nylander.
Oliver Ekman-Larsson has started killing penalties: on the ice for 30% of the team’s shorthanded time in 24 games, up from 6% last season.

James Hagens is on injured reserve and has missed the last 5 games. Marat Khusnutdinov has taken his spot beside Elias Lindholm and Casey Mittelstadt. That line has had 67% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 34:15 together, up from 54% with Hagens.

stakes: The Maple Leafs go in tied for seventh in the Atlantic with 19 points, 10 points behind the Bruins, fourth.

BOS.head: The matchup suits the Bruins
BOS.body: Boston has been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately and has home-ice advantage, while Toronto may be without Marchenko. The Maple Leafs’ way back in is a power play that gets going.

TOR.head: The Maple Leafs face a real test
TOR.body: Boston has been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately and has home-ice advantage, while Toronto may be without Marchenko. The Maple Leafs can pull it off if their power play gets going.

story.head: The Maple Leafs need a win
paras: The Maple Leafs are winless in eight (0-7-1), while the Bruins (14-7-1) beat Detroit 4-1 on Nov 18. This is an Atlantic Division matchup, with the Maple Leafs last (tied for 26th in the NHL) and the Bruins fourth (tied for tenth). The Atlantic has been the strongest of the four divisions so far.

The Maple Leafs have played better than their record (.396) says: their chances are worth about .483, mostly because they’re 3-9 in one-goal games. The Bruins’ record (.659) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.584), largely thanks to their goaltending.

The Maple Leafs get their shots through better than anyone (1st), but have had shaky goaltending (31st). They also take a lot of low-quality shots (31st), so the Bruins wait for good looks, but they settle for hopeful ones. On the other side, the Bruins leave the shooting to their forwards (lowest), sit back rather than chase on the forecheck (2nd lowest) and rarely threaten on the penalty kill (31st). Boston has allowed 2.55 goals a game, the fourth fewest in the league. The Leafs’ knack for getting shots through meets a team that blocks a lot.

Auston Matthews (13 G / 19 A / 32 P in 24 GP) leads the Maple Leafs in scoring and is tied for sixth in the NHL, and William Nylander (11 G / 13 A / 24 P in 24 GP) isn’t far behind. For the Bruins, David Pastrňák (10 G / 18 A / 28 P in 22 GP) leads the way in scoring, with a point in five straight games against Toronto.

Jeremy Swayman (10-5-1 / .908 SV% in 16 GS) will likely start for Boston. Toronto has two options in net: Anthony Stolarz (5-4-1 / .904 SV% in 10 GS) and Sergei Bobrovsky (3-9-2 / .873 SV% in 14 GS). They have split the last ten starts, and Stolarz got the last one on Nov 19. It’s anyone’s guess who gets the net.
The Bruins usually control more of the chances than the Maple Leafs do.
